passages.t: Ashdod, and the prophet stripped and barefoot
passages.happening: In the year the chief commander sent by Sargon king of Assyria came to Ashdod and captured it (verse 1), the LORD had already spoken to Isaiah. ‘Go, remove the sackcloth from your waist and the sandals from your feet’ (verse 2). ‘And Isaiah did so, walking around naked and barefoot’ (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
This is a dated prose story set among the poems against the nations, and one of the best documented events in Isaiah. Ashdod was one of the main Philistine cities on the coast. Around 713 BC its king withheld tribute from Assyria, and Sargon II replaced him. The people of Ashdod put another man, Yamani, on the throne, who stirred up neighboring states to revolt and sought help from Egypt, by then ruled by the Kushite kings. Around 711 BC Sargon's army, led by his chief commander, captured Ashdod. Sargon's own inscriptions report that Yamani fled toward Egypt and Cush, and that the Kushite king later handed him over in chains. Sargon's records also suggest that Judah was among the states the rebels approached.

For centuries Sargon was known only from this verse, and some doubted he existed. Excavations begun in the 1840s at Khorsabad in northern Iraq uncovered his capital, with his palace and inscriptions.

Sackcloth was a coarse garment of goat hair worn by mourners, and sometimes by prophets as a sign of grief over the people's sin. The Hebrew word for naked can mean fully unclothed, but it is also used of someone stripped of the outer garment and wearing only a loincloth, and many interpreters think that is meant here.
passages.later: Micah too went ‘barefoot and naked’ as he mourned his people's coming ruin (Micah 1:8). And Jeremiah later wore a yoke as a sign: ‘Make for yourself a yoke out of leather straps and put it on your neck’ (Jeremiah 27:2).
passages.asks: Isaiah did what God asked, though it cost him his dignity. Ask what obedience might cost you in how others see you. And ask whether you would follow God's word if it made you look foolish.

passages.t: A sign against Egypt and Cush
passages.happening:
Then the LORD explains. ‘Just as My servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush’ (verse 3), so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old, naked and barefoot, to Egypt's shame (verse 4).

‘Those who made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast will be dismayed and ashamed’ (verse 5). On that day the people of this coastland will say, look what has happened to the ones they fled to for help against the king of Assyria. How can they escape now (verse 6)?
passages.hearers:
The sign was drawn from real practice. Assyrian palace reliefs show prisoners of war being marched away stripped and barefoot, and deporting conquered peoples was standard Assyrian policy. To show Egypt and Cush, the proud southern powers, reduced to this was to show their total humiliation.

The chapter gives a concrete example of what chapters 18 and 19 said in poetry: Egypt and Cush cannot save anyone. The episode is a small version of the larger crisis to come, when Hezekiah would be tempted to lean on Egypt against Sennacherib. The fate Isaiah foretold came some decades later, when the Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt in the 670s and 660s BC, took Memphis and Thebes, and carried away captives.

The coastland of verse 6 is Philistia, and perhaps Judah with it. The question they ask is the one Isaiah wants Judah to ask before it is too late.
passages.later: Ezekiel later acted out God's word in his own body as well: ‘lie down on your left side and place the iniquity of the house of Israel upon yourself’ (Ezekiel 4:4). A psalm gives the chapter's lesson: ‘Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save’ (Psalm 146:3).
passages.hard:
Did God really command Isaiah to go naked for three years?

Readers have found this command troubling. Several points help. The Hebrew word for naked is used for being partly clothed as well as fully unclothed, and many interpreters think Isaiah wore only a loincloth, which would still have been deeply humiliating. The three years may describe how long the sign's meaning lasted, the period of the Ashdod crisis, rather than continuous public nakedness; some suggest he appeared this way at intervals. Prophetic sign-acts were often extreme on purpose, and similar things were asked of Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Hosea. The point was to shock a complacent audience.

The difficulty should not be explained away. It fits a pattern in which God's messengers carried in their own bodies the message they preached. It is not a pattern for anyone to shame another person, or to be shamed, in God's name.
passages.asks: Those who made Cush their hope were left asking how they could escape. Ask what you have made your hope that could leave you asking the same. And ask what it would look like to make God your hope before the crisis comes.
